The Red bandfish (Cepola macrophthalma) is a strikingly elongated benthic species inhabiting muddy and sandy substrates across the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Field surveys indicate that males and females both attain a maximum total length of 80 cm [Li = 80 cm], a dimension that places them among the largest members of the Cepolidae family. This remarkable elongation is accompanied by a laterally compressed body and a characteristically long, tapering tail, adaptations that facilitate rapid burrowing into soft sediments. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analyses suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic length after several years of steady somatic expansion, with the most pronounced increases occurring during the first three to four years of life. The slender morphology of the species, combined with its reduced fin spines and extensive dorsal and anal fin bases, reflects a life style centered on excavating and occupying vertical burrows in fine-grained substrates, from which it emerges to feed on zooplankton and small benthic crustaceans.

Reproductive development in Cepola macrophthalma begins relatively early in ontogeny, with the onset of gonadal maturation occurring once individuals reach a total length at puberty of 21.9 cm [Lp = 21.9 cm]. Histological examinations of the gonads reveal that both sexes begin gametogenesis at this size threshold, corresponding approximately to the second or third year of life depending on local thermal regimes. This length at maturity is modest relative to the species ultimate size, representing roughly a quarter of the maximum recordable total length, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous strategy in which early investment in reproduction is prioritized over extended somatic growth. Field collections across the Mediterranean indicate that puberty is attained slightly earlier in warmer southern basins, though the 21.9 cm figure appears robust across most studied populations. The initiation of reproductive activity is accompanied by a shift in energy allocation, with a greater proportion of ingested resources directed toward gonad development and vitellogenesis in females.

At a stable water temperature of 11.9 °C [T = 11.9 °C], typical of the species deeper distributional range during the reproductive season, spawning females release small, pelagic eggs following a synchronized broadcast spawning event. The daily maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the number of oocytes shed per female per day, has been estimated at approximately 301 oocytes per day [Ri = approximately 301 oocytes per day], a value derived from ovarian fecundity counts and observed spawning frequencies under controlled laboratory conditions. This daily output is partitioned across multiple spawning events throughout the protracted breeding season, which may extend from late spring through early autumn. The relatively modest per-event fecundity is offset by the extended duration of reproductive activity, allowing females to gradually deplete their ovarian reserves over several months. Environmental factors, particularly food availability and temperature stability, strongly modulate the realized reproductive rate, with captive individuals maintained under these same thermal conditions displaying the highest sustained oocyte production.

The embryonic development of Cepola macrophthalma begins within small, transparent pelagic eggs that are released into the water column following external fertilisation. Hatchlings emerge from the chorion as yolk-sac larvae possessing a minimal initial somatic mass, with the wet weight at birth measured at approximately 0.000074 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000074 grams]. This exceedingly low birth mass corresponds to an egg diameter of roughly 0.53 mm, among the smallest recorded for any Mediterranean perciform fish, and reflects a reproductive strategy emphasizing high fecundity over per-offspring investment. The lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-hatching, undergoing rapid morphological differentiation before the onset of exogenous feeding. The depleted yolk reserves are absorbed within approximately three to five days at ambient temperatures, after which the developing larvae must successfully capture planktonic prey to sustain further growth. This narrow window between yolk exhaustion and first feeding represents a critical period of high mortality in the early life history.

Longevity records for Cepola macrophthalma indicate that individuals maintained under stable thermal conditions typical of their natural habitat, specifically at 11.9 °C [T = 11.9 °C], can survive for up to 2,920 days [am = up to 2,920 days], which is notable among small-to-medium sized benthic teleosts and suggests a relatively slow pace of senescence. This maximum lifespan, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith age estimates, allows for multiple reproductive seasons, with mature individuals spawning annually over a period of several years. Age-specific mortality rates appear low during the adult phase, increasing markedly only after the seventh year, when signs of physiological decline become evident in both sexes. The combination of an early onset of puberty, modest body size, and multi-year reproductive window aligns with a life-history strategy that balances current reproductive output against the probability of surviving to future breeding opportunities. Predation pressure from demersal piscivores likely imposes a ceiling on realized longevity in wild populations.
